title: Groundnut Toffee
author: Fran Osseo-Asare
desc: Half a cup of sugar with two tablespoons of water, cooked on medium WITHOUT STIRRING until it turns brown — then the nuts go in off the heat.
longDesc: The Ghanaian toffee, and its method differs from brittle in one important way: the sugar is cooked with water and is not stirred at all once it is dissolved. Three quarters of a cup of dry roasted unsalted peanuts are coarsely crushed between two sheets of waxed paper. Half a cup of sugar and two tablespoons of water go into a saucepan and are stirred briefly on medium-high just until the sugar is mostly dissolved, then left on MEDIUM WITHOUT STIRRING until the mixture turns brown — probably around ten minutes. Off the heat, the nuts are stirred in quickly and the toffee is turned onto a wetted board and pressed flat.
ingredients: // For the coconut version: 3/4 cup dried, unsweetened flaked or grated coconut in place of the peanuts, toasted first.
// Water or a little margarine or butter, for the board and the spatula
equipment: Heavy saucepan — one source reading gives 2 quart
Rolling pin or meat tenderiser, and waxed paper or a bag
Glass cutting board or a lasagne or cake pan
Cookie sheet, for the coconut version
steps: Coarsely crush the peanuts — easiest between 2 pieces of waxed paper or in a plastic or paper bag — with a rolling pin or other heavy object like a meat tenderiser.
Wet a glass cutting board or pan, like a lasagne or cake pan, with a little water and set it aside.
Also wet the spatula, spoon or knife, or rub a little margarine or butter on it, and set it aside too.
Put the water and sugar into the saucepan and briefly stir on medium-high heat just until the sugar is mostly dissolved.
Turn it to medium and let it continue cooking on MEDIUM WITHOUT STIRRING it at all until the mixture turns brown — probably around 10 minutes.
When it is a nice golden brown, remove the pan from the heat, turn off the stove, and quickly stir in the nuts.
Immediately turn the toffee onto the wet cutting board and use the prepared spatula or knife to press it flat.

As the candy cools it will harden. Break it into pieces, or score it while still warm into squares, diamonds or triangles and break them off when hard, or take small spoonfuls of the warm — but not hot — candy and roll it into balls.

// For the coconut version: preheat an oven to 350 degrees Fahrenheit, spread the coconut on a cookie sheet and toast it, shaking the pan every couple of minutes. It will probably take only 4 to 6 minutes to lightly toast. Then follow the same caramel method, adding the toasted coconut in place of the peanuts.
chefTips: WITHOUT STIRRING is the instruction she capitalised, and it is the difference between toffee and a grainy mess. Once the sugar is dissolved, leave the spoon out of it.
Wet the board and the spatula BEFORE you start the sugar. There is no time to find them once the nuts are in.
A nice golden brown, at around ten minutes. The time is a guide; the colour is the cue.
The warm-but-not-hot window is the only time you can roll it into balls. Miss it and you are breaking shards instead.
Score it while warm if you want neat squares or diamonds. Scoring does nothing once it has set.
The water is what makes this toffee rather than brittle — two tablespoons, and it lets the sugar dissolve evenly before it colours.
The coconut version uses the identical caramel: four to six minutes of toasting at 350, shaking every couple of minutes, then into the same syrup.
commonMistakes: Stirring the syrup while it colours.
Preparing the board after starting the sugar.
Waiting for dark brown, by which point it is bitter.
Trying to roll balls from hot candy, or from set candy.
Scoring it after it has hardened.
sources: Adapted from 'Candy (toffee), Ghana-style: Recipes #44 Groundnut "cakes and #45 Coconut "cakes"', betumiblog.blogspot.com, Thursday 25 February 2010. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Posted by Fran at 10:15 PM', timestamped 2010-02-25T22:15:00-05:00. Confirmed across three fetches (TWO-PASS).

A MISPRINT IN THE POST TITLE ITSELF, reproduced above exactly as printed and not corrected: the quotation marks are unbalanced — 'Groundnut "cakes' opens a quote and never closes it, while 'Coconut "cakes"' is balanced. TWO-PASS confirmed in that malformed state.

#44 GROUNDNUT TOFFEE, ingredients exactly as printed: '3/4 cup dry roasted unsalted peanuts'; '1/2 cup of sugar'; '2 Tablespoons of water'. Note the capital T in 'Tablespoons' as printed. Yield: NONE PRINTED.

THE CRITICAL INSTRUCTION, verbatim with its original capitals: 'Put the water and sugar into the saucepan and briefly stir it on medium high heat just until the sugar is mostly dissolved. Turn it to medium and let it continue cooking on MEDIUM WITHOUT STIRRING it at all until the mixture turns brown (probably around 10 minutes).'

THE DONENESS CUES, all verbatim: 'just until the sugar is mostly dissolved'; 'until the mixture turns brown (probably around 10 minutes)'; 'When it is a nice golden brown, remove the pan from the heat'; 'As the candy cools it will harden'; and the rolling window, 'take small spoonfuls of the warm, but not hot, candy, and roll it into balls'. This is a colour-driven recipe and it is unusually well specified for a 2010 blog post.
NO CANDY-THERMOMETER STAGE and no numeric syrup temperature are printed. The endpoint is colour.

A CONFLICT ON THE PAN, both readings recorded and neither chosen: one pass gives 'heavy 2-quart saucepan'; the verbatim pass renders step four as 'Put the water and sugar into THE saucepan', implying the pan was specified in an equipment line above the numbered steps that the verbatim pass began below. The 2-quart figure is therefore SINGLE-PASS.

TWO SAFETY NOTES that appeared on one pass only and are therefore SINGLE-PASS: rotate the pan gently if it is browning unevenly, and do not touch it with bare hands because it is very hot. The second is reproduced in the method in the collection's own words since it is a burn risk; neither is quoted as source text.

#45 COCONUT 'CAKES', ingredients exactly as printed: '3/4 cup dried, unsweetened flaked or grated coconut'; '1/2 cup of sugar'; '2 Tablespoons of water' — the sugar and water identical to #44. Method as printed: 'Preheat an oven to 350 degrees farenheit (medium heat). Put 3/4 cup dried, unsweetened flaked or grated coconut onto a cookie sheet and toast it in the oven, shaking the pan every couple of minutes. It will probably take only 4-6 minutes to lightly toast the coconut...Follow the instructions above for making the carmelized sugar syrup, but instead of adding peanuts, add the toasted coconut, then follow the same steps.'

WHY #45 IS A VARIATION HERE AND NOT ITS OWN ENTRY: both verbatim passes independently confirmed that #45 PRINTS NO SEPARATE NUMBERED STEPS AT ALL. It gives only the coconut-toasting step and then cross-references #44 for everything else. Publishing it as a standalone entry would mean inventing a method it does not have, so it is published as the documented variation it is.
SPELLINGS AS PRINTED, not corrected: 'farenheit' and 'carmelized'. Both TWO-PASS.

CULTURAL REMARKS as printed: 'Ghanaians use available ingredients to create simple candies, or "toffees."' And the author reports sending the candies with her husband to distribute at Penn State: 'No candy came home with him.'
NO YIELD is printed for either recipe. The eight servings above is an editorial reading of three quarters of a cup of nuts plus the syrup.

RELATIONSHIP TO NKATE CAKE at GHA116: both are caramelised sugar with groundnuts, but the methods genuinely differ. This one dissolves the sugar in two tablespoons of water and forbids stirring; the nkate cake melts sugar dry over low heat and stirs it occasionally. This one is Ghanaian-sourced; that one is not. Published as two entries on that basis.
storage: 2 weeks in an airtight tin once completely cool. Humidity makes it sticky.
healthBenefits: Peanuts supply protein, niacin, magnesium and vitamin E.
The coconut version supplies medium-chain fats and fibre.
culturalNote: Every West African country makes a version of sugar and nuts, and the Ghanaian one is called toffee whether or not it contains any dairy. The author's line about it — that Ghanaians use available ingredients to make simple candies — is the whole story of a sweet with three ingredients and no equipment.
